The Best Adventure Motorcycle Routes UK 2026 Has to Offer

An adventure bike is happiest when a ride refuses to sit in one category. The best adventure motorcycle routes UK riders can reach do exactly that, threading proper A-road pace into rough moorland singletrack, remote Highland glens and the odd legal green lane where the tarmac simply runs out. I have ridden a Transalp, an Africa Twin and a Tenere across most of these over the past few seasons, and what unites them is space, surface variety and that glorious feeling of being somewhere genuinely wild. This is a bike built for the long game, so these routes reward you for taking the scenic option every single time.

Below I have picked the roads and regions that make an ADV bike sing. Each one names the road, gives you a sense of the distance and character, flags the highlights and points you at a cafe or stop where it makes sense. Pack layers, plan your fuel and give yourself far more time than the mileage suggests.

The A82 Through Glencoe and Rannoch Moor

If you only ride one road in Scotland, make it the A82 as it climbs onto Rannoch Moor and drops into Glencoe. The moor section is a wide, exposed sweep across one of the last true wildernesses in Britain, and the descent through Glencoe itself, past the Three Sisters, is jaw-dropping. It is roughly 30 miles of proper adventure-bike terrain from Bridge of Orchy to Glencoe village, with long sightlines, flowing curves and weather that can turn on a sixpence. The upright riding position of an adventure bike lets you drink in the mountains rather than staring at the vanishing point.

Stop at the Glencoe Cafe or the Real Food Cafe in Tyndrum on the way in for the best fish and chips in the Highlands. This is not a road to rush. Ride it early to beat the coaches.

The A87 to Skye and the Kylerhea Detour

The A87 runs from Invergarry across to the Skye Bridge, and it is a magnificent adventure route in its own right, sweeping past Loch Cluanie and through Glen Shiel beneath the Five Sisters. Once on Skye, adventure riders should peel off the main drag onto the tiny single-track road over the Bealach Udal to Kylerhea, where a small turntable ferry crosses back to the mainland in summer. That detour, all loose edges and hairpins, is exactly the sort of low-speed technical riding that separates an ADV bike from a road tourer.

The Isle of Skye motorcycle guide covers the island loop in full. A bike like the Honda Africa Twin or the Yamaha Tenere 700 is in its element here.

Bealach na Ba and the Applecross Peninsula

The Bealach na Ba is the crown jewel of UK adventure roads. This former drovers pass climbs from sea level at Applecross to 626 metres in a series of tight, gated hairpins that feel more Alpine than Scottish. It is single-track, steep, and utterly committing, with gradients touching 20 percent and passing places that demand constant awareness. The reward at the top is a panorama across to Skye and the Outer Hebrides that few roads in Britain can match.

Ride the Bealach na Ba with humility. It is not a race track. It is a technical mountain road where clutch control, throttle discipline and reading the road ahead matter far more than outright speed. Get it right and it will be the finest half hour of your touring year.

The Applecross Inn at the foot of the descent is a legendary biker stop with fresh seafood and a view over the bay. Time your ride to arrive for lunch.

The North Coast 500 Loop

No adventure round-up is complete without the NC500. This 516-mile loop around the northern Highlands stitches together the wildest coastal and mountain roads in Scotland, from the switchbacks of the north coast to the empty single-track of Assynt and Sutherland. It is best tackled over several days, and an adventure bike with luggage and a comfortable seat is the ideal tool. Expect everything from smooth fast A-roads to gravel-strewn passing places.

  • Best clockwise or anticlockwise: Anticlockwise saves the dramatic west coast for last.
  • Fuel planning: Stations are sparse in the far north. Fill up whenever you see one.
  • Timing: May and September dodge both midges and peak coach traffic.
  • Surface: Some sections are rough and patched, exactly why an ADV bike suits it.

Our NC500 5 day itinerary breaks the whole loop into manageable days with the best stops flagged.

Green Lanes and Legal Byways

The thing that truly sets adventure riding apart is the option to leave the tarmac entirely. Britain has a network of legal unsurfaced byways, known as BOATs and green lanes, where you can ride a road-legal bike on genuine off-road terrain. The Peak District, the Yorkshire Dales, Wales and the Ridgeway in southern England all offer superb legal green laning for those who do their homework on rights of way. Keep it legal, keep it respectful and keep your speed down around walkers and horses.

If you are new to it, read our best green lanes UK guide before you set off. It covers where to ride legally and how to behave responsibly on shared byways. An adventure bike with knobbly-biased tyres like the Aprilia Tuareg 660 transforms these lanes from an ordeal into a highlight.

The A686 Over Hartside

Back on tarmac, the A686 from Penrith to Alston over Hartside Summit is one of the finest fast adventure roads in northern England. It climbs to 580 metres through open fell country in a glorious sequence of sweeping bends, with a cafe at the top that is a magnet for bikers of every stripe. On an adventure bike you can cover the 20-odd miles at a genuinely rapid pace while still soaking up the enormous views west to the Lake District.

The full route features in our A686 Hartside Pass guide. Combine it with the nearby moorland roads for a superb day loop from the M6 corridor.

Building Your Adventure Route

The magic of adventure touring is that these roads link together into epic multi-day trips. A big-tank bike like the BMW R 1250 GS or a lighter middleweight will both do the job, and the choice comes down to how much rough stuff you want to tackle. For a full run-down of the terrain, see our companion guide on how to tour on an adventure bike, and for more Highland inspiration our best motorcycle roads Scotland guide is packed with ideas.

Whichever route you choose, the adventure ethos stays the same. Take the long way round, be prepared to change plans when the weather turns, and never pass a fuel station in the Highlands with less than half a tank. These are the best adventure motorcycle routes UK riding has to offer, and every one of them rewards the bike that refuses to be boxed in.
keyTakeaways: The best UK adventure routes blend fast A-roads, remote singletrack and the odd legal green lane.
Scotland dominates: the A82 through Glencoe, the A87 to Skye, the Bealach na Ba and the 516-mile NC500.
The Bealach na Ba climbs to 626 metres in Alpine-style hairpins from Applecross, the crown jewel of UK ADV roads.
England adds the fast A686 over Hartside to a 580-metre summit cafe.
Legal green laning (BOATs and byways) is possible in the Peaks, Dales, Wales and along the Ridgeway; ride only confirmed rights of way.

faq.q: What is the single best UK adventure road?
faq.a: The Bealach na Ba is the crown jewel. This former drovers' pass climbs from sea level at Applecross to 626 metres in tight, gated hairpins that feel more Alpine than Scottish, with gradients touching 20% and passing places demanding constant awareness. Ride it with humility as a technical mountain road, not a race track, and reward yourself at the Applecross Inn.

faq.q: How long does the NC500 take?
faq.a: The North Coast 500 is a 516-mile loop around the northern Highlands, best tackled over several days rather than rushed. An adventure bike with luggage and a comfortable seat is the ideal tool for its mix of fast A-roads and gravel-strewn single-track. Ride anticlockwise to save the dramatic west coast for last, and target May or September to dodge midges and coach traffic.

faq.q: Can I legally ride off-road in the UK?
faq.a: Yes, on the network of legal unsurfaced byways known as BOATs and green lanes, where a road-legal bike may ride genuine off-road terrain. The Peak District, Yorkshire Dales, Wales and the Ridgeway all offer superb legal green laning if you research the rights of way first. Keep it legal, keep your speed down around walkers and horses, and behave respectfully.

faq.q: How do I plan fuel in the Highlands?
faq.a: Stations are sparse in the far north, so fill up whenever you see one and never pass a Highland fuel station with less than half a tank. On the NC500 and the west coast, the gaps between stations can be considerable, and some keep short hours. Plan your fuel around the remote sections such as Assynt, Sutherland and the north coast.

Anything from a middleweight to a big-tank flagship works, and the choice comes down to how much rough stuff you want. A Honda Africa Twin or Yamaha Tenere 700 excel in the Highlands, while the knobbly-shod Aprilia Tuareg 660 transforms green lanes. For long multi-day trips a big-tank BMW R 1250 GS shines, though a lighter middleweight is easier on the rough stuff.
